items.title: Top fund manager warns most software firms won't survive AI

featured_image.name: Fund Beating 99% of Peers Sees Few Software Firms Surviving ...

items.description:
A fund manager whose portfolio has outperformed 99% of competitors is sounding the alarm on software stocks, warning that artificial intelligence poses an existential threat to the industry and that only a handful of companies will survive the coming disruption.

"We think application software faces an existential threat from AI," said Nick Evans, whose $12 billion global technology fund at Polar Capital beat 99% of peers over the past year and 97% over five years, in comments reported by Bloomberg on Sunday.[1]

The warning comes as software stocks have suffered a brutal start to 2026. An exchange-traded fund tracking the U.S. software sector has plummeted more than 21% this year, according to data from S3 Partners, while hedge funds have generated $24 billion in profits by betting against the sector. The software industry has seen roughly $1 trillion wiped from its market capitalization since late January, sparked by fears that AI large language models could disintermediate traditional enterprise applications.[2][3][4]

items.title: EU's Kallas rejects US criticism, urges Europe to 'reclaim agency'

featured_image.name: Kaja Kallas attends Munich Security Conference | News | ERR

items.description:
The 62nd Munich Security Conference concluded Sunday with European leaders sending a clear message: the continent must take greater responsibility for its own defense amid shifting transatlantic dynamics. Over three days of discussions, top officials outlined plans for increased military spending, nuclear deterrence cooperation, and reduced dependence on Washington.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas rejected American criticism of Europe, pushing back against suggestions that "woke and decadent Europe" faces "civilizational erasure." Speaking at the conference's closing session, Kallas outlined three priorities: defending Europe starting with Ukraine, securing the neighborhood through EU enlargement, and building global partnerships. She warned that Russia "must not gain more at the negotiating table than it has achieved on the battlefield."[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Russia offers to halt strikes if Ukraine holds elections

featured_image.name: Russia revives election-day truce offer, proposes UN rule for Ukraine

items.description:
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin announced Saturday that Moscow is prepared to suspend airstrikes on election day if Ukraine holds presidential polls, reiterating an earlier offer from President Vladimir Putin while questioning the legitimacy of President Volodymyr Zelensky's government.

The announcement comes days before a new round of trilateral talks between Russia, the United States, and Ukraine scheduled for February 17-18 in Geneva, and as Washington continues pressing Kyiv to hold elections as a condition for U.S. security guarantees.

items.title: Rubio backs Orban reelection bid during Hungary visit

featured_image.name: Rubio meets Orbán in Budapest as US and Hungary are to sign ...

items.description:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled to Budapest on Monday to meet with Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, signing a civilian nuclear cooperation agreement and delivering a strong endorsement of the embattled leader just weeks before Hungary's April 12 elections. Rubio told Orban that President Donald Trump is "deeply committed to your success" and that Orban's continued leadership is in America's national interest.[1][2]

The high-profile visit comes as Orban and his Fidesz party face their most difficult electoral challenge since retaking power in 2010. Opposition leader Peter Magyar's center-right Tisza party leads in most polls, with a recent Idea Institute survey showing Tisza at 48% among committed voters compared to 38% for Fidesz.[3]

items.title: India opens AI summit as first major Global South host

featured_image.name: Macron, Lula da Silva among 20 world leaders to attend upcoming ...

items.description:
India kicks off one of the largest artificial intelligence gatherings ever staged as Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurates the India AI Impact Summit 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on Monday. The five-day event, running from February 16 to 20, is the first major global AI summit to be hosted in the Global South, positioning India as a central voice in shaping the future of the technology.[1][2][3]

The summit brings together approximately 20 heads of state and government, including French President Emmanuel Macron, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, along with ministerial delegations from over 45 countries. United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and senior officials from multiple international organizations are also participating.[4][5][6]

items.title: Gold holds above $5,000 as stronger dollar, thin holiday trading weigh

featured_image.name: Gold and silver keep hitting record highs. But is the precious metals market 'broken'?

items.description:
Gold prices edged lower in early trading on Monday but held above the $5,000-per-ounce mark as a stronger dollar and profit-taking weighed on the precious metal following last week's inflation-driven rebound. Trading volumes remained thin with U.S. markets closed for Presidents Day and Chinese exchanges shut for Lunar New Year celebrations.[1][2][3]

Spot gold slipped 0.4% to around $5,020 per ounce in early Monday trading, according to The Business Times. The pullback came after the metal recovered from mid-week lows near $4,880 to close above $5,040 on Friday, buoyed by softer-than-expected U.S. inflation data.[4][5][6]

items.title: Iran proposes energy and mining deals ahead of Geneva talks

featured_image.name: Iran's Araghchi slams European powers for 'irrelevance' in nuclear ...

items.description:
Iran is seeking a nuclear agreement with the United States that would deliver economic benefits for both nations, an Iranian diplomat said Sunday, days before a second round of talks between Tehran and Washington scheduled for Tuesday in Geneva.

The discussions encompass potential business opportunities in oil and gas fields, mining investments, and even aircraft purchases, according to Hamid Ghanbari, deputy director for economic diplomacy at Iran's foreign ministry, as reported by the semi-official Fars news agency and wire service Reuters. Ghanbari argued that the 2015 nuclear pact with world powers had failed to secure American economic interests. "For the sake of an agreement's durability, it is essential that the U.S. also benefits in areas with high and quick economic returns," he said.[1][2][3]

items.title: Netanyahu demands Iran dismantle nuclear infrastructure in US deal
items.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared Sunday that any nuclear agreement between the United States and Iran must include the complete dismantling of Iran's nuclear infrastructure, not merely a pause on uranium enrichment. The demand comes ahead of a second round of US-Iran talks scheduled for Tuesday in Geneva.

Speaking at the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations' 51st Annual National Leadership Mission in Jerusalem, Netanyahu outlined specific conditions he conveyed to President Donald Trump during their White House meeting last week. "There shall be no enrichment capability — not stopping the enrichment process, but dismantling the equipment and the infrastructure that allows you to enrich in the first place," Netanyahu said, according to Reuters.[1]

items.title: Satellite images reveal China expanding nuclear sites in Sichuan

featured_image.name: Satellite images show China working on nuclear propulsion ...

items.description:
Satellite imagery has revealed rapid expansion at Chinese nuclear weapons facilities in Sichuan Province, signaling an accelerating effort to modernize Beijing's arsenal as global arms control frameworks weaken.

The images, first reported by The New York Times on Saturday, show construction activity at several secretive facilities built during the Cold War, including sites believed to be involved in producing plutonium cores for warheads and testing the high explosives needed to trigger nuclear detonations.[1][2][3]

The developments come just ten days after the New START treaty between the United States and Russia expired on February 5, leaving no binding limits on strategic nuclear weapons for the first time since 1972.[4][5]
